\chapter{Overhead --- Daybreak, Sky, Cloud, Star, Shade}
\label{ch:lo-de-arriba}
\hlchaptermodality{289}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the daybreak, the sky, a cloud, a star and the shade in Spanish.}

Complete ES-C289-sombra: name all five overhead in order, from first light to the shade under a tree.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el amanecer]{el amanecer — the piece hiding inside mañana}

\label{lesson:ES-C289-amanecer}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what are the pieces of \emph{expetere}? (\emph{Ex-}, out, and \emph{petere}, to ask.) And what does \emph{la llegada} name? (The arrival.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hasta mañana — a word you have been saying for a long time, with a piece of this one inside it.
  \item el día — what this is the beginning of.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-ma-ne-CER}, stress on the very end. The \emph{c} before \emph{e} is the soft one. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el amanecer} — \textquotedblleft{}the daybreak,\textquotedblright{} the moment it gets light.

Take it apart and Latin \textbf{mane} falls out, meaning \textquotedblleft{}in the morning.\textquotedblright{} Around it sit \emph{a-}, towards, and \emph{-ecer}, an ending that means a thing beginning to happen. So: moving towards morning, and not yet arrived.

You already own that middle piece. \emph{Mañana} is \emph{mane} too, worn down through \textbf{hora maneana}, \textquotedblleft{}the morning hour,\textquotedblright{} until only the \emph{mañ-} was left. Two words you would never have paired, and the same Latin sits in both.

The cousins in English arrive by a different road. \textbf{Matins} is the morning office. A \textbf{matinee} is the showing early enough to still count as morning, at least when somebody named it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word for the moment a day starts, and a piece you can now hear in a word you already had.

That is worth more than one word. Once \emph{mane} is visible inside \emph{mañana}, the two stop being separate things to remember and become one thing wearing two coats.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el amanecer}
  \item \emph{mañana}, then \emph{el amanecer}, and hear \emph{man-} in both
  \item \emph{hasta mañana}, then \emph{el amanecer}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{mane} mean? (In the morning.) Which word you already had carries the same piece? (\emph{Mañana}.) And what does \emph{-ecer} add? (That a thing is beginning to happen.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el cielo]{el cielo — the ceiling over everything}

\label{lesson:ES-C289-cielo}



\begin{quote}
Two back: what does \emph{la despedida} name? (The farewell.) And what did \emph{mane} mean? (In the morning.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el amanecer — what happens up there first.
  \item azul — what it usually is.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CIE-lo}, stress on the first part. The \emph{ie} is one slide, not two beats, and the \emph{l} stays bright to the end. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el cielo} — \textquotedblleft{}the sky.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{caelum}, and the Romans used it for the sky and for the vault of heaven without much worrying which they meant. Spanish kept both senses in the one word.

The English relatives came in by two doors. Through French \emph{ciel} you get \textbf{ceiling} — the sky of a room, which is a nicer thought than the word usually gets credit for. Straight from Latin you get \textbf{cerulean}, the deep blue in a paint box, from \textbf{caeruleus}, \textquotedblleft{}sky-coloured.\textquotedblright{}

Notice what the \emph{ie} is doing. Latin had a short \emph{e} in \emph{caelum}, and Spanish broke it into \emph{ie} the way it did in \emph{bien} and \emph{tiene}. Once you hear that, a whole set of words stops looking irregular.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two words, and both of them are about what is over your head.

\emph{El amanecer} is a moment; \emph{el cielo} is a place. Between them you can already say when and where without any of the machinery a sentence usually needs.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cielo}
  \item \emph{el cielo azul}
  \item \emph{el amanecer}, then \emph{el cielo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{caelum}? (The sky.) Which English word for the top of a room is the same one? (\emph{Ceiling}.) And what colour is \emph{cerulean}? (Sky blue.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la nube]{la nube — where nuance comes from}

\label{lesson:ES-C289-nube}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what was \emph{caelum}? (The sky.) And which piece of \emph{amanecer} means \textquotedblleft{}in the morning\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Mane}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el cielo — where these are.
  \item blanco — what colour they usually are.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{NU-be}, stress on the first part. The \emph{u} is the pure one, and the \emph{b} between vowels is soft, the lips barely meeting. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la nube} — \textquotedblleft{}the cloud.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{nubes}, and it has come down almost untouched: four letters in, four letters out.

The good English relative is not obvious. French took \emph{nubes} and made \textbf{nue}, a cloud, and from \emph{nue} built \textbf{nuance} — which meant the shading of one cloud into another before it ever meant a shade of meaning. When you say a distinction has nuance, you are borrowing a description of the sky.

\textbf{Nebulous} looks like a relative and is a slightly different one: Latin \textbf{nebula} was mist rather than cloud. Close cousins, different words, and the pair is worth keeping apart in your head.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and they stack: a moment, the place above you, and the things crossing it.

\emph{El amanecer}, \emph{el cielo}, \emph{la nube}. Notice that none of the three has needed a new ending or a new pattern — they are ordinary words, and you can already hang \emph{azul} or \emph{blanco} on the last two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la nube}
  \item \emph{la nube blanca}
  \item \emph{el amanecer}, \emph{el cielo}, \emph{la nube}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What English word for a fine distinction began as a shading of cloud? (\emph{Nuance}.) What did \emph{nebula} mean, as against \emph{nubes}? (Mist, not cloud.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la estrella]{la estrella — stella, with a running start}

\label{lesson:ES-C289-estrella}



\begin{quote}
Quick pass: what was \emph{nubes}? (A cloud.) What was \emph{caelum}? (The sky.) And what does \emph{el amanecer} name? (The daybreak.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el cielo — where you find them.
  \item la noche — when you find them.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{es-TRE-lla}, stress in the middle. The \emph{rr} is not here — this is a single \emph{r} after a \emph{t}, one tap. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la estrella} — \textquotedblleft{}the star.\textquotedblright{}

Underneath it is Latin \textbf{stella}, and English took that one bare: something \textbf{stellar} is of the stars, and a \textbf{constellation} is a set of them standing together.

So where did the \emph{e-} come from? Spanish does not care for a word that opens with \emph{s} and another consonant, and it puts an \emph{e} in front to give the tongue somewhere to start. You have seen it without being told: \emph{escuela}, \emph{estudiante}, \emph{España}. Each one is a Latin word with a step built in front of it.

That is why an English speaker learning Spanish and a Spanish speaker learning English trip over the same threshold from opposite sides.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and one small piece of machinery that costs nothing and pays constantly.

\emph{El amanecer}, \emph{el cielo}, \emph{la nube}, \emph{la estrella}. The last of them handed you a way to guess at words you have not met: strip the \emph{e-}, and a Latin or English relative is often sitting underneath.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la estrella}
  \item \emph{estudiante}, \emph{España}, \emph{estrella} — the same step three times
  \item \emph{el cielo}, \emph{la nube}, \emph{la estrella}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{estrella} without its \emph{e-}? (\emph{Stella}.) Why is the \emph{e-} there? (Spanish wants a vowel before \emph{s} plus a consonant.) Name two more words that do it. (\emph{Escuela}, \emph{estudiante}, \emph{España}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la sombra]{la sombra — what an umbrella is little of}

\label{lesson:ES-C289-sombra}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what was \emph{stella}? (A star.) What was \emph{nubes}? (A cloud.) And why does \emph{estrella} begin with an \emph{e}? (Spanish wants a vowel before \emph{s} and a consonant.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el árbol — a reliable source of one.
  \item el cielo — what has to be clear for there to be any.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SOM-bra}, stress on the first part. The \emph{m} closes the lips and the \emph{b} opens them again, so the two run together. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la sombra} — \textquotedblleft{}the shade,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the shadow.\textquotedblright{}

Two Latin words squeezed into one: \textbf{sub}, under, and \textbf{umbra}, shadow. To be \emph{sub umbra} was to be under the shadow, and Spanish ran the phrase together until it named the thing itself.

\textbf{Umbra} is generous in English. An \textbf{umbrella} is a little shadow you carry — built for sun before it was ever built for rain, which the name still admits. To take \textbf{umbrage} is to be put in the shade by somebody. And a \textbf{sombrero} is Spanish handing the word back: a shadow-maker for your head.

The \emph{-ero} on \emph{sombrero} makes a thing that does a job, the way \emph{cocinero} names somebody who cooks. A hat that shades is a \emph{sombrero}, and now the hat is not a word you have to memorise.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{el amanecer}, \emph{el cielo}, \emph{la nube}, \emph{la estrella}, \emph{la sombra}.

Read them in order and they run from first light to the dark shape under a tree — a whole day's worth of overhead, in five words and no new grammar at all. Three of the five handed you something extra on the way out: a piece of \emph{mañana}, the \emph{e-} step, and now an ending you had already met wearing a different hat.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la sombra}
  \item \emph{sombra}, then \emph{sombrero} — the shade and the thing that makes it
  \item all five in order — \emph{el amanecer}, \emph{el cielo}, \emph{la nube}, \emph{la estrella}, \emph{la sombra}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin words are inside \emph{sombra}? (\emph{Sub}, under, and \emph{umbra}, shadow.) Which English words still carry \emph{umbra}? (\emph{Umbrella}, \emph{umbrage}.) And what does \emph{-ero} do? (Names somebody or something that does the job.)
\end{tcolorbox}
